# Syphilis Self-Testing: Rethinking Access to Diagnosis

January 2, 2026

$~$

One of the things that concerns me about syphilis is that we already know how to cure it, but infections continue to rise in many parts of the world. The <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/sexually-transmitted-infections-(stis)"><span class="blog-link-text">World Health Organization estimates</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> that the number of new syphilis infections worldwide among adults aged 15 to 49 increased from 7.1 million in 2020 to **8 million** in 2022.

Like many sexually transmitted infections, <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/syphilis"><span class="blog-link-text"><strong>syphilis doesn't always cause noticeable symptoms</strong></span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>. People may have the infection for some time without knowing it. Without testing, the infection can go untreated and potentially be passed on to others.

Having lived in both the Philippines and Canada, I have seen how much getting care can depend on what is available nearby and what someone can afford.

I have continued to explore these issues through my work on infectious disease diagnostics. In 2025, I co-authored a <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://doi.org/10.1128/jcm.00982-25"><span class="blog-link-text"><strong>commentary in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology</strong></span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> with Professors <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/aboutus/people/marks.michael"><span class="blog-link-text">Michael Marks</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>, <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/aboutus/people/tucker.joe"><span class="blog-link-text">Joseph Tucker</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>, and <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/aboutus/people/peeling.rosanna"><span class="blog-link-text">Rosanna Peeling</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> on the role of syphilis self-testing in prevention and control.

One of the questions we explored was who might be missing out on testing through conventional diagnostic services.

### When testing depends on the clinic

In Canada, getting tested for syphilis often involves visiting a healthcare provider and <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/infectious-diseases/sexual-health-sexually-transmitted-infections/canadian-guidelines/syphilis/screening-diagnostic-testing.html"><span class="blog-link-text">having a blood sample collected for laboratory testing</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>. The results are then used to determine whether further assessment or treatment is needed.

For many people, this approach works well. But someone who lives several hours away from a clinic might need to take time off work and pay for transport just to get tested, particularly if another appointment is needed. Someone else might live close to a clinic but worry about being recognised there.

Both might benefit from having the option to test somewhere other than a clinic.

### What is syphilis self-testing?

**Syphilis self-testing** allows people to test themselves outside a clinic, including at home. Most self-tests use a small blood sample collected through a finger prick and provide a result within minutes.

In August 2024, the <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-marketing-authorization-enables-increased-access-first-step-syphilis-diagnosis"><span class="blog-link-text"><strong>United States Food and Drug Administration authorised the country's first at-home, over-the-counter syphilis test</strong></span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>. The <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240090767"><span class="blog-link-text"><strong>World Health Organization also published recommendations in 2024</strong></span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> suggesting that self-testing be offered as an additional approach to syphilis testing.

### What have we learned from research?

A <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003930"><span class="blog-link-text">randomised controlled trial published in 2022</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> recruited 451 men who have sex with men (MSM) across 124 cities in China. Participants hadn't been tested for syphilis in the previous six months. Researchers compared conventional testing services with free dual HIV and syphilis self-tests delivered by post, with or without a lottery-based financial incentive.

Over the six-month study period, approximately 63% of MSM in the self-testing group without the lottery incentive got tested for syphilis, compared with around 15% of those receiving the usual testing services.

What stood out to me was that nearly 80% of those who self-tested reported never having been tested for syphilis before.

The trial took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, when restrictions on clinic-based testing may have increased demand for self-testing.

In Zimbabwe, a <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://doi.org/10.1071/SH23038"><span class="blog-link-text">randomised controlled trial published in 2023</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> recruited 100 participants in Harare through community-based organisations working with MSM. Researchers compared community-based syphilis self-testing with facility-based testing.

Testing uptake was 74% among those offered self-testing and 58% among those referred to a healthcare facility. However, the study didn't provide enough evidence to establish a difference between the two approaches.

The researchers also found that self-testing cost less per person tested from the service provider's perspective.

Of the six participants who received a reactive (positive) self-test result, four returned for confirmatory testing. Being able to complete the initial test didn't guarantee that everyone would receive further testing.

### A self-test isn't the same as a diagnosis

Most syphilis self-tests detect antibodies that the body produces in response to the bacterium that causes syphilis. These antibodies can remain detectable long after an infection has been successfully treated.

A reactive self-test result may indicate a current or previously treated infection. False-positive results are also possible. <a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/infectious-diseases/sexual-health-sexually-transmitted-infections/canadian-guidelines/syphilis/screening-diagnostic-testing.html"><span class="blog-link-text">Further testing and clinical assessment are needed</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a> to determine whether treatment is necessary.

The timing of testing matters too. Someone who has recently acquired syphilis may not yet have developed enough antibodies for the test to detect. If you have symptoms or think you've been exposed to syphilis, seek medical advice promptly, even if your self-test result is negative.

### Making self-testing work in practice

If self-tests are only available for purchase online or in pharmacies, people who can't afford them may still be left out. Distributing free or subsidised tests through community-based organisations could help extend their reach.

Some people might want help using the test, while others would prefer to do it on their own.

<a class="blog-source-link" href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240096394"><span class="blog-link-text">HIV self-testing has taught us that providing someone with a test kit is only part of the work</span><span class="blog-link-arrow" aria-hidden="true">&nbsp;↗</span></a>. Someone who receives a reactive result at home needs to know where to go for further testing. Even if they do, they may encounter the same difficulties that made accessing clinic-based testing challenging in the first place.

We have evidence that self-testing can increase testing uptake. What we still need to understand is whether it helps people get diagnosed and treated sooner.

I don't see self-testing as a replacement for laboratories or existing sexual health services. It's another way for people to begin accessing those services.

I would like someone who tests for syphilis at home to have as clear a route to treatment as someone who gets tested at a clinic.

–Ayel
